discovery: Optical lattice atomic clocks reaching 10^-18 precision and accuracy

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

motivation: Katori conceived the optical lattice clock, trapping many neutral atoms at a 'magic wavelength' so that the trapping light leaves the clock transition unperturbed. He and Ye then made the idea work, and it has become the most precise measuring instrument ever built. Ye's strontium clocks reached a total uncertainty below 10^-18 and, through spin-squeezed and imaged ensembles, resolved the gravitational redshift across a single millimetre-scale atomic sample. Katori's transportable clocks measured relativistic height differences in the field. Both lines of work pushed noise down toward fundamental limits and then used that sensitivity to ask physical questions: about general relativity, drifts in the fundamental constants and dark matter. This is measurement science at its finest. Ingenious device physics produced a new window on nature, and the work is now driving a redefinition of the SI second. The two made complementary and decisive contributions.
